title: Earth Was Built From Its Own Backyard, Scientists Say
summary:
Imagine baking a cake. For years, scientists thought some of the flour came from a store far, far away. Now a new study says: nope. Earth was baked from ingredients in its own neighborhood.

Earth sits in the inner Solar System — the closer part, near the Sun. Some scientists thought 6 to 40 percent of Earth's building blocks drifted in from beyond Jupiter, way out in the cold. That idea helped explain where Earth's water came from.

But two scientists in Switzerland, Paolo Sossi and Dan Bower, checked the numbers again. They looked at isotopes in many meteorites. Isotopes are like sibling atoms — same element, but different weights. Think of identical twins where one is a little heavier.

Their result? Earth's material came entirely from the inner Solar System. Outer material is less than 2 percent of Earth's mass — maybe zero.

"We were truly astonished," Bower said.

Why does it matter? It means Earth's water was probably here all along, close to the Sun. And Jupiter may have acted like a giant wall, blocking stuff from drifting inward. Earth grew up in a quiet, steady neighborhood.
why_it_matters: This explains where the water in your drinking glass and in every ocean may have come from — and it helps scientists figure out which faraway planets could have water and life too.

background_read: Earth was born about 4.5 billion years ago, when dust and rock swirling around the young Sun stuck together and grew into a planet.
Jupiter (the biggest planet in our Solar System, much farther from the Sun than Earth) is so heavy that its gravity can pull space rocks toward it or push them away.
Scientists study meteorites (space rocks that landed on Earth) because they are leftovers from the time the planets were forming.
Article_Structure: WHO: Two scientists in Switzerland, Paolo Sossi and Dan Bower, who checked the numbers again and studied isotopes in many meteorites.
WHAT: They found that Earth's building blocks came entirely from the inner Solar System, with outer material making up less than 2 percent of Earth's mass — maybe zero.
WHERE: Earth, in the inner Solar System near the Sun; the study looked at meteorites and at Jupiter's possible role as a barrier.
WHY: It suggests Earth's water was probably here all along, close to the Sun, and that Jupiter may have blocked material from drifting inward.

perspectives.description: Paolo Sossi and Dan Bower say they were 'truly astonished' — their numbers show Earth was built from nearby material, which is a simpler story than the old idea.
Some scientists believed 6 to 40 percent of Earth came from beyond Jupiter, and that this helped explain Earth's water. They may want more meteorite samples before giving up that idea.
Science works by checking new measurements against old ones. Many will want other teams to test the same numbers before calling the question settled.
